title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 81–82
description: Advanced writing and typographic conventions, indirect speech, vague reference, informal quantities and tactful conversational language.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Target vocabulary and distinctions follow its teaching pages and exercises; Portuguese translations, usage notes and example sentences are independently written. Original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete teaching pages for Units 81–82, styled formatting examples, sections A–B and A–D respectively, exercises 81.1–81.4 and 82.1–82.6, and associated answer-key entries. Exercise-only additions are identified separately.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA only for relatively short entries checked with high confidence or explicitly transcribed in the book. Multi-word targets generally omit IPA rather than fabricate connected-speech detail.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing content and metadata is in English except for Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared target vocabulary, distinct senses, styles, illustrations, exercises and answer-key material against the supplied Advanced third-edition PDF. Reviewed newly written examples, context notes and Portuguese renderings. JSON structure, unique IDs, required fields, provenance and static TTS text constraints were checked programmatically.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 audio. Browser import, voice synthesis output and speech-recognition quality were not tested. Vague placeholders and indirect expressions are context-sensitive; some forms may be inappropriate in professional, formal or respectful conversation.

units.title: Unit 81 — Writing: style and format
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 168–169 (PDF pages 170–171).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Communication · writing, typography and document layout
learningObjectives: Choose precise verbs for rapid notes, drafting, copying, revising and writing up academic work.
Describe electronic document production, typography, punctuation marks and page formatting.
Distinguish fonts, typefaces, font sizes, text emphasis and the hierarchy of headings.
Use writing and formatting terminology appropriately in academic and professional contexts.

sectionsChecked: A · Aspects of writing and usage explanations
B · Type and print, layout illustration and typography examples

items.example: She scribbled a reminder on the back of the receipt before leaving.
items.note: Implies writing quickly and with little care for neatness.

items.example: The report's chatty opening felt out of place in a formal submission.
items.note: A chatty writing style resembles friendly conversation; unsuitable in some formal documents.

items.example: During the lengthy briefing, he doodled patterns along the edge of his notes.
items.note: Drawing or writing aimlessly while your attention is elsewhere.

items.example: The archive acquired an early manuscript containing the poet's handwritten revisions.
items.note: An original text prepared by its author, handwritten or otherwise unpublished.

items.example: Jot down the reference number so you can quote it when you call.
items.note: Usually means write a small amount quickly to help you remember it; informal.

items.example: The trainee copied out the instructions to keep in her laboratory notebook.
items.note: Reproduce written information, typically by writing it again rather than summarising.

items.example: Write down each question before the discussion begins.
items.note: Record something in writing, particularly information you hear or think of.

items.pt: redigir a versão final; preparar um relatório escrito
items.example: The researchers are writing up their findings for a peer-reviewed journal.
items.note: Turn notes, drafts or research into a proper finished written account.

items.example: Please make a note of the revised submission deadline.
items.note: Slightly more formal than jot down; commonly followed by the information to remember.

items.pt: redigir uma primeira versão de uma carta
items.example: Before contacting the supplier, she drafted a letter setting out the complaint.
items.note: Draft is a verb for preparing a preliminary written version for later revision.

items.example: His first draft made a strong argument but needed better evidence.
items.note: A preliminary version; further editing is expected before the final text.

items.example: The novelist sent the corrected typescript to her editor in September.
items.note: A typed manuscript, particularly an author's text before publication.

items.pt: formatar; ajustar a apresentação de um documento
items.example: Format the headings consistently before exporting the report.
items.note: As a verb, arrange text and layout to produce the intended appearance.

items.example: Your access code must contain at least twelve characters.
items.note: In computing and typography, a letter, digit, punctuation mark or other symbol.

items.example: Choose a legible font for the slides rather than a decorative one.
items.note: A design or family of lettering; not the same thing as font size.

items.example: The publisher chose a serif typeface for the printed edition.
items.note: Often used much like font, though technically a typeface is a design family.

items.example: An asterisk after the figure directs readers to a note below the table.
items.note: The star-shaped symbol used for notes, references or special markings.

items.pt: recuar; deslocar o início de uma linha
items.example: Indent each paragraph to make the structure easier to follow.
items.note: As a verb, start the line farther from the usual left margin.

items.example: The footnote number appears as a superscript after the quotation.
items.note: Small characters positioned above the normal text line, often for notes or exponents.

items.example: The title should state the subject of the article clearly.
items.note: Main name of a publication, chapter, presentation or other work.

items.example: A concise subtitle can clarify the scope of an academic book.
items.note: Additional title line that explains or qualifies the main title.

items.example: Could you run off a copy of the agenda for the late arrivals?
items.note: In this context, run off means quickly print or reproduce a document.

items.pt: digitar sem olhar para o teclado
items.example: She learned to touch-type so she could take notes without watching her hands.
items.note: Type using the fingers by position, rather than looking down at the keys.

items.example: Cut and paste the paragraph into the section on methodology.
items.note: Move selected electronic content from one position to another.

items.example: Copy and paste the reference into your bibliography, then check the formatting.
items.note: Duplicate selected content while leaving the original in place.

items.example: Increase the font size in the figure labels so they remain readable.
items.note: Size of text, unlike font or typeface, which refers to its design.

items.example: Use bold for the subsection labels, but keep the body text regular.
items.note: Thicker, darker type used to make words more prominent.

items.example: In this referencing style, the names of books appear in italics.
items.note: Slanted type; frequently used for titles, emphasis and specialised conventions.

items.pt: caixa de texto com fundo sombreado
items.example: Put the safety warning in a shaded box so readers notice it.
items.note: A visually distinguished block of text with a coloured or shaded background.

items.example: The proofreader asked for double inverted commas around the direct quotation.
items.note: A British English term for double quotation marks.

items.example: The house style requires double quotation marks for dialogue.
items.note: Another term for double inverted commas; punctuation conventions vary.

items.example: The editor used single quotation marks around the term being defined.
items.note: Also called single quotes; their use depends on the style guide.

items.pt: marcador de lista; item com marcador
items.example: Put each action item on a separate bullet point.
items.note: A bullet is the symbol before a list item; a bullet point may also mean the item itself.

items.example: Place the translation in round brackets after the technical term.
items.note: British term for the punctuation marks ( and ).

items.example: The markup language places certain tags inside angle brackets.
items.note: The signs < and >; the book also calls them diamond brackets.

items.example: The handbook refers to these paired symbols as diamond brackets.
items.note: An alternative label for angle brackets, the signs < and >, as used in the source.

items.example: The editor placed a clarification in square brackets within the quotation.
items.note: The punctuation marks [ and ].

items.example: In many programming languages, curly brackets delimit a block of code.
items.note: The signs { and }; also known as braces.

items.example: Write the application reference in upper case to avoid confusion.
items.note: Upper case refers to capital letters; contrasted with lower case.

items.example: The system treats lower case and upper case as different characters.
items.note: Lower case means small letters, not capital letters.

items.example: The form asks applicants to write their surnames in block capitals.
items.note: Separate, clearly formed capital letters, rather than cursive handwriting.

items.example: The chapter heading describes the main theme of the next section.
items.note: A heading at chapter level, contrasted with a sub-heading within it.

items.example: Use a sub-heading to distinguish the limitations from the results.
items.note: A heading below a larger section or chapter heading.

items.example: Italicise the journal title, but leave the article title in plain text.
items.note: British spelling; American English normally italicize.

items.example: The quotations are indented to separate them from the main argument.
items.note: Describes text beginning farther from the margin than surrounding text.

items.pt: trabalho montado com trechos copiados e colados
items.example: The supervisor rejected the report as a cut-and-paste job with no original analysis.
items.note: Critical, informal description of writing assembled from copied material rather than developed independently.

units.title: Unit 82 — Whatchamacallit: being indirect
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 170–171 (PDF pages 172–173).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Communication · indirectness, vague language and conversational tact
learningObjectives: Interpret vague meanings of thing and get in informal conversation without treating them as interchangeable.
Recognise playful placeholders for forgotten names of objects and people and their social limitations.
Contrast informal large-quantity and small-quantity expressions with more neutral alternatives.
Use indirect or tactful expressions while recognising that wording cannot eliminate potential offence.

sectionsChecked: B · When you cannot recall a word
D · Being indirect and less threatening

items.pt: ter fixação por; ter implicância com
items.example: My colleague has a thing about people arriving late, even by a minute.
items.note: Informal; can imply a strong liking, dislike or preoccupation, depending on context.

items.word: make a big thing of it
items.pt: fazer um grande caso disso; exagerar a importância
items.example: It was a minor typo, but the manager made a big thing of it.
items.note: Informal expression for treating something as much more important than necessary.

items.example: Once the server failed, there wasn't a thing the staff could do until the backup started.
items.note: A thing can mean anything in this emphatic negative construction.

items.example: For one thing, the new proposal would exceed the budget.
items.note: Introduces one reason in a list, often followed by for another thing.

items.example: For another thing, the deadline leaves no time for user testing.
items.note: Adds another reason; for another is a shorter variant.

items.pt: a questão é que; o problema é que
items.example: The thing is, we still haven't received approval for the experiment.
items.note: Informally introduces an explanation, objection or difficulty.

items.pt: do jeito que as coisas estão; na situação atual
items.example: As things are, we cannot promise delivery by Friday.
items.note: Refers to the current situation; as things are at present is a longer form.

items.example: Unless the committee gets it together soon, the event will have to be cancelled.
items.note: Informal; organise yourself or take effective action rather than merely plan.

items.pt: resolver as pendências; pôr as coisas em ordem
items.example: We need to get things sorted out before the inspection begins.
items.note: Arrange matters so that problems have been solved; out can sometimes be omitted.

items.pt: conseguir ficar a sós com ela
items.example: At the conference I finally got her to myself long enough to discuss the project.
items.note: The pronoun changes with the person; means spend time alone with someone.

items.example: There is one thing I would like to raise before we finish.
items.note: Thing can vaguely refer to an issue, subject or matter under discussion.

items.pt: entender; captar uma explicação ou ideia
items.example: I get the technical argument, but I disagree with the conclusion.
items.note: Informal get means understand; distinguish it from get meaning obtain.

items.example: We'll get it in the post first thing tomorrow morning.
items.note: Informal get something in the post means arrange for it to be sent.

items.example: We need to get through the remaining agenda items before noon.
items.note: With tasks or a list, means deal with and finish them; different from pass an exam.

items.example: Although they have different priorities, the two researchers get on with each other.
items.note: In British English, have a good relationship with someone; not the same as get on with a task.

items.pt: sair de férias; conseguir escapar da rotina
items.example: We're hoping to get away for a few days after the project deadline.
items.note: In this context, leave for a break or holiday; not an escape from danger.

items.example: Pass me the thingy that holds the cables together, will you?
items.note: Informal substitute when the object's name escapes you; may also refer to a person.

items.pt: coisa; troço cujo nome não vem à cabeça
items.example: Where did we put the thingummy for tightening that fitting?
items.note: Playful, very informal placeholder for a forgotten object's name; spelling varies.

items.example: He asked for the thingumijig that measures the angle of the joint.
items.note: Very informal and playful; refers to an unnamed or forgotten object.

items.pt: coisa; treco; objeto cujo nome se esqueceu
items.example: I can't find the thingamibob that connects the hose to the tap.
items.note: Informal filler for an object's name; spelling and variants differ.

items.example: Have you seen the whatsit we use to open the back panel?
items.note: Informal replacement for a forgotten name; usually an object.

items.example: Could you fetch the whatchamacallit we use to spread icing?
items.note: Very informal word for something you cannot name at the moment.

items.pt: e coisas do tipo; e outros objetos não especificados
items.example: The cupboard is full of spare adapters, old cables and whatnot.
items.note: Often follows a list to mean other unspecified things; can also serve as a vague noun.

items.pt: fulano; aquele sujeito cujo nome não lembro
items.example: Is whatsisname from the finance department attending the meeting?
items.note: Informal placeholder for a man's forgotten name; can sound dismissive.

items.pt: fulana; aquela mulher cujo nome não lembro
items.example: I spoke to whatsername from the design team about the drawings.
items.note: Informal placeholder for a woman's forgotten name; may sound disrespectful.

items.pt: de sobra; muito; uma grande quantidade de
items.example: We have bags of time to revise the proposal before Monday.
items.note: Informal abundance, especially with time, energy and enthusiasm.

items.pt: um monte de; uma porção de
items.example: A load of unexpected requests arrived just before the release.
items.note: Informal large quantity; often used with singular a load of plus a plural or uncountable noun.

items.example: They received loads of useful feedback from the pilot users.
items.note: Informal equivalent to a lot of; works with countable plural or uncountable nouns.

items.pt: uma grande quantidade de; um monte de
items.example: The archive contains a mass of correspondence from the period.
items.note: Emphasises a large quantity or accumulation; not always informal in every context.

items.example: Masses of visitors turned up despite the heavy rain.
items.note: Informal large quantity; generally followed by plural or uncountable nouns.

items.example: Dozens of applicants attended the information session.
items.note: Can mean several groups of twelve or an approximate large number.

items.example: We've collected tons of evidence to support the recommendation.
items.note: Very informal exaggeration, not necessarily a literal weight.

items.example: I have explained the procedure umpteen times this week.
items.note: Humorous or mildly exasperated informal determiner meaning very many.

items.example: I have a bit of a headache, so I may leave the meeting early.
items.note: Informal small amount; a bit of a before singular countable descriptions is also common.

items.pt: um mínimo de; nem um pouco de
items.example: She offered no scrap of evidence for the accusation.
items.note: Often in negatives for even a tiny amount; no scrap of work is an emphatic criticism.

items.pt: não é exatamente a ideia mais prática
items.example: Your proposal is not the most practical idea given the safety constraints.
items.note: Understatement that softens a negative judgement; other adjectives can replace practical.

items.word: I mean that in the nicest possible way
items.pt: digo isso com a melhor das intenções
items.example: That approach may be rather expensive, and I mean that in the nicest possible way.
items.note: Attempts to soften criticism; can sound ironic or insincere depending on tone.

items.example: No offence intended, but the conclusion seems to overlook the key evidence.
items.note: Precedes or follows potentially critical remarks; it does not guarantee they will not offend.

items.word: if you don't mind me saying so
items.pt: se você me permite dizer; se não se importa que eu diga
items.example: If you don't mind me saying so, the introduction could be much shorter.
items.note: A polite preface to advice or criticism; informal-spoken and moderately tactful.

items.pt: pelo que entendi; fiquei sabendo que
items.example: I gather the timetable has changed, although nobody has confirmed it.
items.note: Suggests information inferred or heard indirectly, without claiming first-hand certainty.

items.example: Incidentally, have you received the revised agenda for tomorrow?
items.note: Introduces a loosely related point or a change of subject in conversation.

items.pt: com exceção dos presentes; sem incluir vocês
items.example: Most consultants charge far too much, present company excepted, of course.
items.note: A potentially humorous way to exclude the people present from a criticism.

items.pt: inclusive eu; incluindo a mim mesmo
items.example: Several members of the team, myself included, underestimated the workload.
items.note: Explicitly includes the speaker in a group, often while sharing responsibility.
